headline: Sakana AI's Fugu orchestrates multiple LLMs as a single API, dynamically assembling specialist agents
summary: Sakana AI's Fugu acts as a learned manager, intelligently routing tasks and stitching together outputs from a pool of specialist models, offering a single API for complex multi-agent orchestration.
details: Sakana AI's Fugu represents a shift in AI, moving beyond single massive models to coordinate a pool of strong, specialist models. Presented as a single API, Fugu intelligently routes tasks, assigns roles, and combines outputs from multiple frontier LLMs.

This multi-agent orchestration system tackles the complex production challenges of AI, such as selecting the right model, verifying outputs, splitting tasks, and optimizing for cost-effective calls. Fugu turns these orchestration problems into its core product.

The system dynamically assembles agents from various vendors, allowing users to opt out of specific models for privacy or compliance. This approach maintains a simple API while enabling a much smarter backend coordination than hand-built routers.

Fugu differentiates tasks, routing easier subtasks to lighter agents and reserving heavier agents for complex problems like deep reasoning or security analysis. This ensures that not every task incurs the highest computational cost.

Its workflow involves a learned coordination process where Fugu decides agent participation, roles, and exchange procedures. The system discovers effective collaboration patterns that human operators might not readily identify.

Fugu is built upon two ICLR 2026 papers, TRINITY and Conductor, which demonstrate training systems to orchestrate other models rather than hand-designing workflows. This signifies a broader shift towards smarter model systems.

This approach significantly improves cost-performance by intelligently routing tasks to the most appropriate and cost-efficient agents. It avoids sending every request to the most expensive model in the pool, optimizing resource use.

Reliability is also enhanced, as Fugu's design reduces the brittleness common in agentic systems. By utilizing specialists and deliberate verification roles, it minimizes the ripple effect of single model errors.

Sakana AI offers Fugu as a balanced option for general workloads like coding and interactive work where latency matters. Fugu Ultra is designed for more complex, high-stakes, multi-step tasks such as paper reproduction or security analysis, prioritizing answer quality over speed.

The system reports strong performance across coding, reasoning, science, and agentic benchmarks, comparing well with or even surpassing publicly available frontier models. This highlights the effectiveness of its orchestration-first strategy.

headline_marked: [[36GB memory leak]] in Claude Code server traced to WebAssembly filesystem
headline: 36GB memory leak in Claude Code server traced to WebAssembly filesystem
summary: A Node.js service for Claude Code users experienced a 36GB memory leak over six weeks. The culprit was sql.js, which, when compiled to WebAssembly, failed to deallocate native memory files, leading to hundreds of leaked database copies.
details: A Node/Express service providing a shared memory store for Claude Code users experienced a creeping memory leak, growing to ~36 GB RSS over six weeks before being terminated by the OOM-killer. This classic leak pattern pointed to a significant underlying issue.

Initial process analysis quickly identified the ruflo mcp start child process, which wrapped a stdio MCP server, as the source of the ballooning memory, while the Node/Express proxy remained stable at ~60 MB. This narrowed the investigation to the wrapped process.

Inspecting process.memoryUsage() showed the V8 JavaScript heap was flat at 24 MB, indicating the growth was entirely in native memory, specifically external and arrayBuffers, outside the garbage-collected JS heap. A heap snapshot, though small at ~18 MB, revealed 203 large buffers, each 11 MB.

These 11 MB buffers matched the size of the on-disk memory.db files. The retainer chain pointed to Emscripten's in-memory filesystem (MEMFS), with each buffer identified as a MEMFS file named dbfile_<random>, essentially full copies of the database.

The mechanism involved sql.js's Database constructor writing input bytes into a MEMFS file via FS.createDataFile. However, the Database.prototype.close() method, which unlinks these files (FS.unlink), was not being called.

This meant that when the JavaScript Database wrapper was garbage-collected, the native/WASM memory it allocated within the sql.js module's shared MEMFS was not freed. Each database open without a corresponding close() created a permanent 11 MB leak.

For containment, an RSS watchdog was implemented in the proxy. It monitors the child's RSS and gracefully respawns the child process when a threshold is crossed, effectively dropping the entire bloated MEMFS and bounding memory usage with no dropped requests.

The proper root cause fix involved caching the backend per database path. This ensures the database is opened once and reused, preventing repeated loads and the creation of new dbfile_* instances, thereby eliminating the leak.

An additional lesson learned during recovery from a corrupted database was the importance of backing up all three files in a WAL-mode SQLite database (.db, -wal, -shm). Copying only the .db file leads to "malformed" errors as the latest committed state resides in the WAL.
